name: Chicken Meatballs in Cranberry Sauce

ingredients.buy: 5 cups (three and a half 14 oz cans)

writer_notes: All 17 locked ingredient lines are used by a step and no step uses an unbought item; reconciliation walked both directions.

Source page groups chili powder, cayenne and red-pepper flakes in the sauce; step 4's 'mix cranberry sauce with remaining ingredients' supports placing them in the sauce mix, so they are named in the Mix the cranberry sauce step.
Olive oil locked line shows '7 tbsp; 3 1/2 tbsp' (two pours); prose keeps oil as a searing ingredient only, matching the transcription.
No cost_ps or cost_lines were supplied, so prose uses the ${{cost_ps}} token and carries zero traceable package-cost claims in shop_smart.
Macros used in prose (646 cal, 55 g protein) are taken verbatim from the locked view; no number was computed.
Rosemary is optional garnish but is bought/costed (7 g); it is used in the final step so it is not an orphan.

prose.intro_html:
Every so often a recipe shows up that tastes like a holiday and costs like a Tuesday. This is that recipe. Tender chicken meatballs, seared golden, then simmered in a glossy cranberry sauce that walks the line between sweet and a little bit of heat. It eats like something you would pay real money for at a restaurant, and it comes out of one pan.

Here is what makes it work for meal prep. You are building 14 servings, and each one lands at 646 calories with 55 grams of protein. That is a serious amount of protein for a dinner that feels like comfort food. The cranberry and honey carry the flavor, the chicken carries the numbers, and the whole thing reheats without turning sad. Let me walk you through buying it right and cooking it once.
prose.shop_smart:
A few smart moves before you fill the cart. This batch leans on a handful of pantry spices you probably already own, so read your shelf before you buy duplicates.

  • Chicken breast is the anchor. You need 7 pounds of boneless skinless chicken breast for the full 14 servings. Buy the largest value pack your store stocks rather than the small trays. You are cubing it and running it through a food processor anyway, so shape and size do not matter here. Grab it when it hits its lowest per pound shelf price and you win the whole recipe.
  • Cranberry sauce does the heavy lifting on flavor. The batch calls for 5 cups, which works out to three and a half of the 14 ounce cans. Whole berry or jellied both work, so buy whichever is priced better that week.
  • The spice rack covers most of the seasoning. Chili powder, cayenne, red pepper flakes, garlic powder, onion powder and paprika are all standard pantry jars. Check what you have before you buy anything new.
  • Panko and whole wheat flour are small pours. You use 7/8 cup of each, so a single standard package of either covers this batch with room to spare for the next one.
  • Honey and Worcestershire are pantry keepers. A 7/8 cup pour of honey and a half cup of Worcestershire come off bottles that live in the door of your fridge and the corner of your cupboard for months.
prose.make_it:
This is a food processor recipe, which is the trick that makes it cheap. You are grinding your own chicken instead of paying a premium for the pre ground stuff, and the seasoning goes in at the same time so every bite is flavored all the way through.

  1. Grind and season. Cut the 7 pounds of chicken breast into cubes and add them to the food processor. Pulse a few times to break them down, then add the panko, the beaten eggs, the Worcestershire, the garlic powder, onion powder and paprika, the black pepper and the salt. Pulse again until the meat is medium fine and everything is evenly worked in. Work in batches if your processor is small, because 7 pounds is a lot to crowd into one bowl.
  2. Form and flour. With wet hands, roll the mixture into 1 inch balls. Wet hands are the whole secret here, because the mix will not stick to them. Roll each ball lightly through the whole wheat flour and shake off the excess so you get a thin coat, not a crust.
  3. Sear them off. Heat a large non stick pan over medium and drizzle in olive oil. Add the meatballs in a single layer without crowding, and cook about 2 minutes per side until they are golden brown and cooked through. Do this in batches and set the finished ones aside.
  4. Mix the cranberry sauce. While the meatballs cook, stir the 5 cups of cranberry sauce together in a bowl with the honey, chili powder, cayenne and red pepper flakes, plus a little salt and pepper. Taste it. This is your chance to dial the heat up or down before it hits the pan.
  5. Simmer it all together. Return the meatballs to the pan and pour the cranberry sauce over them. Stir gently to coat, reduce the heat to low, and simmer until the sauce is bubbly and glossy, about 5 minutes. Garnish with fresh rosemary if you are using it.
prose.portion_html:
Here is the honest way to split 14 even servings, and it is the same method I use on every batch. Do not eyeball it. Weigh the empty pan before you cook, then weigh the full pan of finished meatballs and sauce at the end and subtract. Take that cooked weight, divide by 14, and that is your target grams per container.

Scoop meatballs and sauce onto the scale and fill each container to that number. The person who packs the first box and the person who packs the last box should be eating the same dinner. That is how you actually hit 646 calories and 55 grams of protein per serving instead of guessing and getting 10 big portions and 4 sad ones.
prose.cost_closing_html:
So what does it cost to eat like this? This batch comes in at ${{cost_ps}} per serving. Fourteen dinners, each one carrying 55 grams of protein, for the price of a couple of drive through combos. That is the entire pitch of cooking once and eating all week.

Run the math on your own week. A dinner out is easily ten to fifteen dollars before you even think about a drink. Cooking this batch buys you two weeks of lunches or dinners for one person, or a week of dinners for a small household, at a number that does not make you flinch.

Cook once, eat all week, and let the numbers do the arguing.

head.description: Budget meal prep chicken meatballs simmered in a sweet and spicy cranberry sauce. Makes 14 servings at 646 calories and 55 grams of protein each, all from one pan.

steps: Cut 7 pounds of chicken breast into cubes and pulse in a food processor to break them down. Add the panko, beaten eggs, Worcestershire sauce, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, black pepper and salt, then pulse again until the meat is medium fine and evenly seasoned. Work in batches if needed.
With wet hands, roll the mixture into 1 inch balls. Roll each ball lightly through the whole wheat flour and shake off the excess for a thin coat.

Heat a large non stick pan over medium and drizzle in olive oil. Add the meatballs in a single layer without crowding and cook about 2 minutes per side until golden brown and cooked through. Work in batches and set finished meatballs aside.
While the meatballs cook, stir the cranberry sauce together in a bowl with the honey, chili powder, cayenne, red pepper flakes and a little salt and pepper until well combined.

Return the meatballs to the pan and pour the cranberry sauce over them. Stir gently to coat, reduce the heat to low and simmer until bubbly and glossy, about 5 minutes. Garnish with fresh rosemary if using.
